analyzed-feature.name: Analyze, plan & build

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Map the code the request will change so the plan can be precise.
1. Find the entry points and modules involved, and follow the real data and control flow through them.
2. Identify the change surface: the files and symbols that must change, the callers and consumers affected, and any configuration, schema or persisted data involved.
3. Find the patterns to follow: how similar features are built here, naming, error handling and test style. Point at concrete examples.
4. List the tests that cover this area, the commands that run them, and where new tests belong.
5. Name the risks: compatibility, migrations, concurrency, performance, security, and areas you could not make sense of.
Do not change any files. Plan reads your report next and builds the plan on it, so reference concrete files and symbols and keep facts apart from assumptions.

analyzed-feature.description: Builds a change in code that should be understood first: Analyze maps the code and the change surface, Plan writes the plan you approve, Build implements it, and Verify checks every criterion and sends failures back to Build.

focus.plan: Build the plan on the analysis: use its change surface, the patterns it points at and the test locations it found.

implement.name: Build & verify

route.when: The user clearly approves going ahead and wants the change made now: 'do it', 'go ahead and build that', or a specific, already-decided change. This edits files.

implement.description: For a change that is already decided, often a plan from an earlier workflow: Plan adopts or completes it, you approve it, Build implements it, and Verify checks every criterion and sends failures back to Build.

focus.plan: This workflow usually starts once the change is decided. If the context already holds a plan or design the user agreed to (from Architect & plan, Debug & plan a fix or Security audit & fix plan), adopt it: keep its requirements, criteria, tasks and ids, and change only what the code shows is out of date or missing. Otherwise write the plan from the request.

documentation.name: Write documentation

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Find what documentation is needed and what it must say.
1. Identify the audience (users, contributors, operators, API consumers) and what they need to do with the docs.
2. Find the existing documentation: where it lives, its format and conventions, and what is outdated or missing.
3. Find the source of truth for everything to be documented: the symbols, commands, options, configuration and defaults in the code.
4. List the examples the docs need and how each can be checked (a command to run, a test, a compile).
Do not change any files. Plan reads your report next; reference concrete files and symbols.

documentation.description: Writes or updates documentation from the code itself: Analyze finds the gaps and the source of truth, Plan lists what to write for your approval, the docs are written, Verify checks them against the code, and a final review reads them as their audience would.

focus.plan: Name each document or section to write or update, where it lives and who it is for. Criteria include that every statement matches the code and every example and command works.
focus.build: Write for the audience in the plan and follow the existing documentation conventions. Check every statement, name, option and default against the code, and run or compile every example and command you include where you can.
focus.verify: Check every documented name, option, default and behavior against the code, and run or compile the examples and commands where you can. Wrong or stale documentation is fail.
focus.review: Read the docs as their intended audience would: accurate against the code, complete for the task they support, easy to follow, consistent with the rest of the documentation, with working links and examples. Inaccurate content is fail; style preferences are not.

refactor.name: Refactor safely

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Pin down what the refactor must keep.
1. Identify the code to restructure and the goal of the refactor in the request.
2. List the observable behavior and the public interfaces that must not change: functions and types other modules use, outputs, file and data formats, errors.
3. Find the tests that cover that behavior and the commands that run them, and name the gaps where behavior is not pinned by a test.
4. Find every caller and dependent of the code that will move or change.
5. Suggest a safe order of small steps that each keep the project building and the tests passing.
Do not change any files. Plan reads your report next; reference concrete files and symbols.

refactor.description: Restructures code without changing what it does: Analyze pins the behavior and interfaces that must stay the same, Plan splits the refactor into small tasks you approve, each task is built and reviewed on its own, Verify runs the checks, and a final review confirms behavior is unchanged.

focus.plan: Tests that pin behavior not yet covered come first. Every task keeps the project building and the tests passing, and behavior and public interfaces stay the same unless the request says otherwise.
focus.build: Keep observable behavior and public interfaces identical. Run the tests before and after your change; a test may change only for an interface change the plan names, never to make a behavior change pass.
focus.review: Confirm behavior is unchanged: compare the old and new code paths, check every caller still gets the same results and errors, look for dropped edge-case handling, and check the structure improved the way the request intended, with no dead code or leftover duplicates. A behavior change the plan did not call for is fail.

investigate.name: Research & analyze

route.when: The user wants to understand or investigate how some existing functionality works, or how a technology or approach compares, before deciding anything: questions like 'how does X work', 'what are my options for Y', 'where is Z handled'. Nothing needs to change yet.

research.name: Research
research.instructions:
Find out what the user needs to understand or decide, and gather the evidence for it.
1. Restate the question in one or two sentences and list the sub-questions that must be answered before the user can decide.
2. Look at the workspace first: what the project uses today (manifests and lockfiles for libraries and versions, configuration, existing patterns) and which constraints that sets.
3. Where the answer depends on how a library, API, standard or tool behaves, check primary sources: official documentation for the versions in use, changelogs, release notes, issue trackers. Note the version and date of what you rely on.
4. When there are several ways to go, compare them on what matters for this project: fit with the existing code, complexity, performance, security, maintenance, licensing and the cost of switching.
5. Recommend one option, say why, and say what would change your recommendation.
6. Keep verified facts (with a link or a file path) apart from inference, and list what is still uncertain.
Do not change any files. Analyze reads your findings next and maps them onto the code, so name the parts of the codebase your findings touch and the questions only the code can answer.

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Answer the user's question from the code, using the research as a guide.
1. Start from the request and from the questions Research left for the code.
2. Find the entry points and follow the real flow: callers, data structures, state, configuration and error paths. Read the code rather than guessing from names.
3. Answer the question directly first, then give the evidence: a file path and symbol for every claim, with short excerpts only where they make the point.
4. Relate the research to this codebase: which option fits how the code is built, what adopting it would touch, and what it would cost.
5. Call out risks, surprises and anything you could not confirm, and say how to confirm it.
Do not change any files. Your report is the workflow's final result and goes straight to the user, who may continue with a design or a plan from it, so it must stand on its own: lead with the answer and a recommendation, then the supporting detail.

investigate.description: Answers a question about the code or a technology without changing anything: Research gathers sourced options and a recommendation, then Analyze traces how the existing code works and answers the question with file-level evidence.

researched-feature.name: Research, design & build

research.name: Research
research.instructions:
Gather what has to be known before the feature is designed.
1. Restate what the feature must do, and list the open questions that need outside knowledge: libraries, APIs, protocols, standards, platform limits.
2. Check what the project already uses (manifests, lockfiles, existing integrations) so the options fit the stack and versions in place.
3. Research primary sources: official documentation for the versions in use, changelogs, known issues, reference implementations. Note versions and dates.
4. Compare the viable approaches on fit with the codebase, complexity, performance, security, maintenance and licensing.
5. Recommend one, with the reasons and the conditions under which another would be better, and list what is still uncertain.
Do not change any files. Architect designs the feature from your findings next, so give it the facts it needs: API shapes, limits, configuration and pitfalls.

architect.name: Architect
architect.instructions:
Design the feature in this codebase, using the research.
1. Start from Research's recommendation; depart from it only for a reason you state.
2. Read the code the feature will live in: modules, interfaces, the patterns used for similar features, and the tests.
3. Lay out the design: components and responsibilities, interfaces and data shapes, data and control flow, state, error handling, configuration, and how each part is tested.
4. Name the compatibility constraints and the boundaries of the change: which files and modules change and which must not.
5. Order the work into pieces that can each be built and checked on their own.
Do not change any files. Plan turns your design into small tasks, each built by a fresh builder that sees only its own task, so be concrete: real paths, symbols and types.

researched-feature.description: For a feature that needs outside knowledge and a design first: Research gathers sourced options, Architect designs the solution, Plan breaks it into small tasks you approve, each task is built and reviewed on its own, and Verify checks every criterion.

focus.plan: Follow the Architect's design and its order of work.
focus.build: Follow the Architect's design: its interfaces, data shapes and boundaries. If the code makes part of it impossible, do the closest thing that meets the criteria and say what differs.

optimize-performance.name: Optimize performance

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Find where the time or memory really goes, and how to measure it.
1. Identify the slow or heavy path the request is about and the code on it.
2. Find or define a repeatable measurement: an existing benchmark, a profiling command, a timed test or a script, with its input size and conditions.
3. If you can run it, record the baseline numbers together with the command. If you cannot, say how it should be run. Never invent measurements.
4. Identify the likely bottlenecks with evidence (complexity, repeated work, I/O, allocations, locking), ranked by expected gain.
5. Note the behavior that must stay the same and the tests that pin it.
Do not change any files. Plan reads your report next and sets measurable targets.

optimize-performance.description: Makes something measurably faster or lighter: Analyze finds the bottleneck and how to measure it, Plan sets targets you approve, Build measures before and after its change, and Verify checks the numbers and that behavior is unchanged.

focus.plan: Make the measurement part of the plan: a baseline task with the exact command, then the changes, then the same measurement again. Criteria state each target as a comparison with the baseline under the same conditions, plus unchanged behavior.
focus.build: Measure the baseline with the planned command before changing anything, then change the code, then measure again the same way. Report both numbers from real runs only; if a measurement cannot run here, say so and give the command.
focus.verify: Check that the before and after numbers come from the same command and conditions and meet the plan's targets, and rerun the measurement if you can. Run the tests to confirm behavior is unchanged. A claimed improvement without a real measurement is fail, unless measuring is impossible here: then it is manual.

security-remediation.name: Security remediation

audit.name: Security audit
audit.instructions:
Audit the requested scope for real, exploitable security problems.
1. Define the scope and its trust boundaries: who supplies input, what is trusted, where secrets and sensitive data live, what runs with elevated rights.
2. Check the classes of problem that apply: injection (SQL, shell, path, template), missing authentication or authorization, unsafe deserialization, secrets in code, logs or errors, insecure defaults and configuration, misused cryptography, SSRF and open redirects, missing validation at boundaries, and dependencies with known advisories for the versions in use.
3. For each finding give an id (S1, S2, ...), a severity (critical, high, medium, low) with a one-line reason, the file and symbol, the conditions under which it can be exploited, the impact, and a precise remediation with the check that proves it is fixed.
4. Mark each finding confirmed (you traced it in the code) or unverified (a pattern that needs a closer look), and do not inflate severity.
5. Say what you did not cover.
Do not change any files. Plan turns your findings into fix tasks next, and at the end a security acceptance step checks each finding by its id, so the ids must stay stable.

security-remediation.description: Finds and fixes security problems: a security audit ranks the findings, Plan turns them into tasks you approve, each fix is built and reviewed on its own, Verify checks every criterion, and a security acceptance step confirms each finding is really fixed.

focus.plan: Each confirmed finding becomes a requirement under its id (S1, ...) with an acceptance criterion that proves the exploit no longer works; fix the highest severity first. Rotating leaked secrets, deploying and rewriting history are follow-ups for the user, not tasks.
focus.build: Fix the root cause of the finding at the trust boundary, not only the one call site, and do not weaken any other control. Add a test that shows the exploit no longer works where that is feasible.

security-audit.name: Security audit & fix plan

route.when: The user asks whether code is secure, or wants vulnerabilities, risky dependencies, exposed secrets or unsafe configuration reviewed.

audit.name: Security
audit.instructions:
Audit the requested scope for real, exploitable security problems.
1. Define the scope and its trust boundaries: who supplies input, what is trusted, where secrets and sensitive data live, what runs with elevated rights.
2. Check the classes of problem that apply: injection (SQL, shell, path, template), missing authentication or authorization, unsafe deserialization, secrets in code, logs or errors, insecure defaults and configuration, misused cryptography, SSRF and open redirects, missing validation at boundaries, and dependencies with known advisories for the versions in use.
3. For each finding give an id (S1, S2, ...), a severity (critical, high, medium, low) with a one-line reason, the file and symbol, the conditions under which it can be exploited, the impact, and a precise remediation with the check that proves it is fixed.
4. Mark each finding confirmed (you traced it in the code) or unverified (a pattern that needs a closer look), and do not inflate severity.
5. Say what you did not cover.
Do not change any files. Plan reads your findings next and turns them into a fix plan.

security-audit.description: Audits the requested scope for concrete security risks, ranks the findings and plans how to fix them. Nothing is changed; the fix plan can be handed to a build workflow.

focus.plan: Plan the fixes in order of severity. Each confirmed finding becomes a requirement under its id (S1, ...) with an acceptance criterion that proves the exploit no longer works. Unverified findings become investigation tasks or follow-ups. Rotating leaked secrets, changing production configuration and rewriting history are follow-ups for the user, not tasks.

careful-change.name: High-risk change

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Map the change and its blast radius before anything is planned.
1. Find every place the change reaches: the code that changes, its callers and consumers, public interfaces, persisted data and its formats, configuration, background jobs and other services.
2. For each, say what could break and how it would show up.
3. Find what protects it today: the tests that cover it and the commands that run them, types, validation, feature flags, and the gaps.
4. Identify what must not change: behavior other code relies on, data compatibility, the public API.
5. Suggest the safest order of work, how to roll back, and what to test before and after.
Do not change any files. Plan reads your report next and splits the work into small tasks, so reference concrete files and symbols.

careful-change.description: For changes where mistakes are expensive (shared code, data, public interfaces): Analyze maps the blast radius, Plan splits the work into small tasks you approve, each task is built and reviewed on its own, Verify checks every criterion, and a final review looks for regressions before you confirm.

focus.plan: Keep every task small and safe on its own, and put tests that pin current behavior before the change that could break it. Make compatibility and rollback explicit criteria.
focus.build: Change only what your task needs. Keep public interfaces, data formats and behavior other code relies on unless the task says otherwise, and add or run tests for every path you touch.
focus.review: Focus on risk: callers and consumers that may break, data compatibility and migrations, error handling and partial failure, concurrency, and whether a rollback is possible. A regression or an unhandled failure path is fail.

plan-build-verify.name: Plan, build, verify
plan-build-verify.description: The everyday workflow for a change: Plan writes requirements, acceptance criteria and tasks; you approve the plan (your notes revise it); Build implements it; Verify checks every criterion against the workspace and sends failures back to Build; checks only a person can do are given to you to confirm.

check-changes.name: Verify & review changes

route.when: The user wants work that was already done, their own changes or the previous result, checked or reviewed for correctness, regressions and quality, without anything being edited.

verify.name: Verify
verify.instructions:
Run the checks that apply to the changes and give the final verdict.
1. Run the project's checks that cover the changed code (tests, type check, lint, build) with the tools you have: focused tests for the changed areas first, then the wider suite when that is practical.
2. Report each check with the command, whether it passed, and the output that matters. Tell failures the changes caused apart from failures that were already there.
3. Confirm or refute what Review asked you to check.
4. Give the verdict: acceptable, acceptable after fixes, or not acceptable, with Review's blocking findings and any failing checks first.
Do not edit files. Your report is the workflow's final result for the user.

review.name: Review
review.instructions:
Review the changes the user means, without editing anything.
1. Work out which changes are meant: the ones the request names, the result of the previous workflow in the context, or the uncommitted changes in the workspace. Look at the actual code with the tools you have, and say which changes you reviewed.
2. Read every changed file and enough of the surrounding code to judge the change: callers, tests, configuration.
3. Look for wrong behavior and missed edge cases, regressions for existing callers, missing or weak tests, poor error handling, security problems, performance traps, and code that does not follow the project's conventions.
4. Give prioritized findings (blocking, should fix, minor), each with file and line, what is wrong, why it matters, and the fix.
5. Say whether the changes are acceptable as they are.
Verify runs the project's checks next and gives the final verdict with your findings, so list anything it should confirm by running a check.

check-changes.description: Reviews work that is already done (your own changes or the previous result) for correctness, regressions and quality, then runs the project's checks. Nothing is edited; you get prioritized findings and a verdict.

diagnose.name: Debug & plan a fix

route.when: Something is broken or failing and the user wants the cause found: an error message, a failing test, wrong behavior or a regression. A fix plan is wanted, not yet the fix itself.

debug.name: Debug
debug.instructions:
Find the root cause of the failure the user reports.
1. Pin down the symptom: the exact error, failing test, input or behavior, and what was expected instead. Take it from the request and the context; ask the user only if you cannot go on without it.
2. Reproduce it with the smallest check you can: one test, one command, one input. Record the command and its output. If you cannot reproduce it, say what you tried and what is missing.
3. Trace from the symptom to the cause: read the code on the failing path, form hypotheses, and test each against evidence (outputs, logs, code paths). Keep what you observed apart from what you suspect.
4. State the root cause with file and line, why it produces the symptom, and since when if that is visible (a recent change, a dependency update).
5. Specify the regression test: where it goes, what it does, and that it fails today and should pass after the fix.
6. Note other places with the same defect, and what the fix must not break.
Do not edit files or install dependencies; describe the fix instead. Plan reads your diagnosis next and turns it into the fix plan.

diagnose.description: Finds the cause of a failure (an error, a failing test, wrong behavior) by reproducing it, then plans the fix and its regression test. Nothing is changed yet.

focus.plan: Plan the fix for the root cause in the diagnosis, not a workaround for the symptom. The first task adds the regression test the diagnosis specifies (it fails today), the next fixes the cause, and the plan covers the other occurrences the diagnosis found. One criterion is that the regression test passes.

design.name: Architect & plan

route.when: The user has a requirement or earlier findings and wants a design or an ordered implementation plan before any code is written: 'how should we build X', 'plan this', 'design the approach'. Often the follow-up after an investigation.

architect.name: Architect
architect.instructions:
Design how the request should be built in this codebase.
1. Restate the goal, the constraints the user gave, and the decisions already made in the context.
2. Read the code the design will live in: the modules, their interfaces, the patterns used for similar features, and the tests.
3. Lay out the design: components and their responsibilities, interfaces and data shapes, data and control flow, where state lives, error and failure handling, and how each part is tested.
4. Where there is a real choice, compare at least two approaches and explain the one you pick: why it fits this codebase, what it costs, what it rules out.
5. Name the compatibility constraints (public APIs, persisted data, configuration, migrations) and the boundaries of the change: which files and modules change and which must not.
Do not change any files. Plan reads your design next and turns it into requirements and ordered tasks, so be concrete: real paths, symbols and types, not generic advice.

design.description: Turns a requirement or earlier findings into a design and an ordered implementation plan before any code is written. Nothing is changed; the plan can be handed to Build & verify.

focus.plan: Turn the Architect's design into the plan and keep its choices. Where the code contradicts part of the design, say so and plan what the code allows.

bug-fix.name: Fix a bug

debug.name: Debug
debug.instructions:
Find the root cause of the failure the user reports.
1. Pin down the symptom: the exact error, failing test, input or behavior, and what was expected instead. Take it from the request and the context; ask the user only if you cannot go on without it.
2. Reproduce it with the smallest check you can: one test, one command, one input. Record the command and its output. If you cannot reproduce it, say what you tried and what is missing.
3. Trace from the symptom to the cause: read the code on the failing path, form hypotheses, and test each against evidence (outputs, logs, code paths). Keep what you observed apart from what you suspect.
4. State the root cause with file and line, why it produces the symptom, and since when if that is visible (a recent change, a dependency update).
5. Specify the regression test: where it goes, what it does, and that it fails today and should pass after the fix.
6. Note other places with the same defect, and what the fix must not break.
Do not edit files or install dependencies; describe the fix instead. Plan writes the fix plan from your diagnosis next, and Build implements it.

bug-fix.description: Fixes a failure end to end: Debug reproduces it and finds the root cause, Plan writes the fix and its regression test for you to approve, Build adds the test and fixes the code, and Verify confirms the test passes and nothing else broke.

focus.plan: Plan the fix for the root cause in the diagnosis, not a workaround for the symptom. The first task adds the regression test the diagnosis specifies (it fails today), the next fixes the cause, and the plan covers the other occurrences the diagnosis found. One criterion is that the regression test passes.
focus.build: Write the regression test first and run it to see it fail for the reason in the diagnosis. Then fix the root cause, run it again to see it pass, and run the tests around the changed code. Report both runs.
focus.verify: Confirm that the regression test exists, exercises the reported failure and passes; that the fix addresses the root cause in the diagnosis rather than hiding the symptom; and that the tests around the changed code still pass.

specify.name: Specify a change

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Understand the change and the code it touches, so the spec describes this project and not a generic one.
1. Read the context: the project file with its principles, the capabilities that already exist, the change record, and the current spec if there is one. The request may add notes from the person; they are the latest word.
2. Work out what the change is for and who it is for. Take the answer from the request, the context and the code; do not ask the person unless you cannot go on without it.
3. Read the code the change would touch: modules, public interfaces, data, existing behavior that the change must keep, and the tests that show how it works today.
4. List what is already decided, what is genuinely unclear (only questions the person can answer, not things the code can answer), and which existing capabilities the change adds to or changes.
Do not change any files. The next step writes the spec from your findings, so be concrete: real paths and names, and mark clearly what you observed and what you assume.

spec.name: Write spec
spec.instructions:
Write the spec of the change as the file spec.md. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Use exactly this structure and these headings:

# <Title of the change>

## Why
Why this change is needed, in a few sentences.

## What changes
What will be different when this is done.

## User stories
- As a <who>, I want <what>, so that <why>.

## Requirements

### R1: <A requirement, as a short statement>
Capability: <capability name> (adds "<Requirement name>")
<One or two sentences of detail.>

- C1: WHEN <situation> THEN <observable result>.
- C2: WHEN <edge or failure case> THEN <observable result>.

## Out of scope
- <What this change deliberately does not do.>

## Clarifications
- <date>: <question that was answered>? <answer>.

## Open questions
- <A question only the person can answer.>

2. Every requirement has an id (R1, R2, ...) and at least one criterion (C1, C2, ... numbered across the whole file). A criterion is something a person who was not here can check: WHEN a situation THEN an observable result. Include the edge and failure cases that matter.
3. The Capability line says which capability the requirement adds to or changes, using the names of the existing capabilities where they fit; leave it out for a requirement that belongs to no capability.
4. Put under Open questions only what the person must decide. If the code or the context answers a question, answer it in the requirement instead.
5. When the context holds a current spec.md, revise it instead of starting over: keep its ids, keep everything the person wrote or edited, apply the notes in the request, and move each open question the notes answer to Clarifications together with its answer.
Describe what the system must do, not how to build it: files, classes and steps belong to the design, which is written next. Do not change any files; the spec is saved from your reply.

specify.description: Writes the spec of a change into its folder: Analyze reads the project, the existing capabilities and the code, then the spec is written with requirements, criteria and open questions for you to answer. Nothing else is changed.

spec-plan.name: Design & tasks for a spec

architect.name: Design
architect.instructions:
Write the design of the change as the file design.md. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Read the context: the project file and its principles, the spec of the change (requirements and criteria), and any current design to revise. Decisions in Clarifications are made; open questions the person has not answered need an assumption you state.
2. Read the code the design will live in: the modules, their interfaces, the patterns used for similar features, and the tests.
3. Use these headings: `## Approach` (the choice and why; compare at least two options where there is a real choice), `## Components and files` (what is added or changed, with real paths and symbols), `## Data and contracts` (types, storage, interfaces, compatibility), `## Failure handling`, `## Testing` (which test proves which criterion), `## Principles check` (each principle of the project file, and how this design keeps it), `## Risks`.
4. When a current design.md is in the context, revise it: keep what the person wrote and change only what the spec now requires.
The next step breaks your design into tasks, so be concrete: real paths, symbols and types, not generic advice. Do not change any files; the design is saved from your reply.

tasks.name: Tasks
tasks.instructions:
Break the design into the ordered task list of the change as the file tasks.md. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Use exactly this format, one line per task with its instructions indented below it:

# Tasks: <number> <title>

- [ ] **T1** <Task title>. R1 (C1, C2)
  <What to change: files, symbols, the pattern to follow, the tests to add.>
- [ ] **T2** <Task title>. R1 (C3) after T1
  <Instructions.>

2. Every task has an id (T1, T2, ...), names the requirement (R) and the criteria (C) of the spec it satisfies, and lists the tasks it must come after. Every criterion of the spec is named by at least one task.
3. A task is one coherent piece that leaves the workspace working and fits in one builder session, so a large change is several tasks. Order them so each builds on the ones before it; tests belong in the task whose behavior they prove.
4. The instructions name the files and symbols to change, the pattern to follow and the tests to add, concretely enough that a smaller model can build the task without exploring.
5. When a current tasks.md is in the context, keep every task that is ticked (`[x]`) exactly as it is, keep the ids of the rest where they still apply, and add or change only what the spec and design now require.
Do not change any files; the task list is saved from your reply.

spec-plan.description: Turns the spec of a change into its design and an ordered task list in the change folder: Design reads the spec and the code and checks the project's principles, then Tasks breaks it into small tasks that name the criteria they satisfy. The files are the result; you can edit them before building.

implement-spec.name: Implement a spec
implement-spec.description: Builds a change from its folder: the unticked tasks of tasks.md are built one at a time (a step plan, a builder and a review for each), then Verify checks every criterion of spec.md and you try what only a person can check. Finished tasks are ticked in the folder as the work goes, so a stopped run continues after them.

focus.build: The tasks, criteria and design come from the change folder; follow the design where the code allows, and do not edit the specs folder: the host ticks tasks and writes the task documents.
focus.verify: Check every criterion of spec.md against the workspace, not only those of the tasks built in this run.

start-specs.name: Survey the project

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Work out what this repository is and what it does, so the project file and the capability specs describe the real thing.
1. Read the request and the context: any project file and capability specs that already exist are to be revised, not replaced. If the repository has little or no code, the request is the description of the project to write the specs for.
2. Read the repository: the README, the manifests and build files, the entry points, the main modules and their public interfaces, the tests and the CI configuration. Use repo_overview and project_info where they help.
3. Work out the project's purpose and users, its stack and the real commands to build, test and run it, the conventions the code follows, and any principles it plainly keeps (for example error handling or testing rules).
4. Group what the system does into capabilities: coherent areas a person would name (a feature area or a subsystem), usually between three and ten. For each one note its purpose and the behaviors it provides, taken from the code and the tests.
Do not change any files. The next steps write the project file and the capability specs from your findings, so be concrete and mark what you observed apart from what you assume.

project.name: Write project file
project.instructions:
Write the project file as the file project.md. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Use exactly these sections:

# <Project name>

## Purpose
What this project is for, and who uses it.

## Stack
Languages, frameworks, and where the code lives.

## Commands
How to install, build, test and run it (the real commands).

## Conventions
Naming, structure, error handling, testing: what a new change must follow.

## Principles
Rules every change is checked against. Few, and each one testable.

2. State only what the analysis supports. Commands must be the real ones; leave out what you could not confirm instead of guessing.
3. When the context holds a current project file, revise it: keep what the person wrote and change only what is wrong or missing.
Do not change any files; the file is saved from your reply.

survey.name: List capabilities
survey.instructions:
Propose the capabilities of the repository as a list the person reviews, as the file onboarding.md. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Use exactly this structure, one `## ` section per capability:

# Onboarding: capabilities of <project name>

Edit this list, then write the capability specs. Delete an entry to skip it; copy an entry to add one.

## <capability-name>
Purpose: <one sentence: what this part of the system is for>
Paths: `<folder or file to start reading>`, `<another>`
Notes: <optional: what is tricky, what must not be missed, what to leave out>

2. A capability is a coherent area a person would name: a feature area or a subsystem, not a layer or a single file. Aim for three to twelve; fewer, broader ones for a small project. The name is a short lowercase word or hyphenated words and becomes the folder under capabilities/.
3. Paths must be real: only list files and folders you saw in the repository, the ones where reading should start (the main module, its public interface, its tests). Two to five per capability is enough.
4. Notes are for what the next step could miss: a part that is easy to get wrong, behavior that lives outside the listed paths, what belongs to another capability. Leave Notes out when there is nothing to say.
5. When the context holds a current capability list, revise it: keep every entry the person edited or added, keep the names, and only add what the code now shows or correct what is wrong.
The next step writes one spec per entry, each in its own run that reads the code at the listed paths, so the list decides what gets specified. Do not change any files; the list is saved from your reply.

start-specs.description: Surveys an existing project: Analyze reads the repository (or, for a new project, your description), then the project file is written and the capabilities are proposed as a list in onboarding.md for you to edit. Nothing else is written until you ask for each capability's spec.

onboard-capability.name: Write a capability spec

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Understand one capability of the system from its code, so its spec says what the system really does.
1. Read the context: the project file, this capability's entry in the survey (its purpose, the paths to start from and the person's notes), the other capabilities, and the current spec if there is one.
2. Read the code at the listed paths and follow it where it leads: the public interface, the data it keeps, what it calls and who calls it, and the tests, which show the intended behavior. Stay inside this capability; leave the others' ground to them.
3. List the behaviors the capability provides, each with the normal case and the edge and failure cases the code handles or its tests check. Note what you observed apart from what you assume.
Do not change any files. The next step writes the spec from your findings, so be concrete: real names and the behavior of each, not how it is built.

spec.name: Write capability spec
spec.instructions:
Write the spec of the capability as the file spec.md. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Use exactly this structure:

# <Capability title>

Purpose: <one sentence: what this part of the system is for>

## Requirements

### Requirement: <Name of the requirement>
<One or two sentences of what the system does.>

#### Scenarios
- WHEN <situation> THEN <observable result>.
- WHEN <edge or failure case> THEN <observable result>.

2. Describe what the system does now, as requirements a person can check, taken from the code and its tests: not what it could do and not how it is built. Each requirement has a name that stays stable (later changes refer to it by name) and scenarios in WHEN … THEN form for the normal case and the edges the code handles.
3. Keep it focused: a handful to a dozen requirements. A requirement you cannot support from the code does not belong in it. You may name the files a behavior lives in, in backticks, only if they exist.
4. When the context holds a current spec, revise it: keep its requirement names and everything the person wrote, and add or correct only what the code shows.
Do not change any files; the spec is saved from your reply.

onboard-capability.description: Writes the spec of one capability from the code at the paths the survey listed for it: Analyze reads that part of the system and its tests, then the spec is written as named requirements with scenarios. One run per capability.
